thread.title: Experts raise concerns over FIFA's air quality plans for 2026 World Cup venues
thread.title_full: Experts raise concerns over FIFA's air quality plans for 2026 World Cup venues

author: beaver state news
title: Experts raise concerns over FIFA's air quality plans for 2026 World Cup venues
text:
The 2026 World Cup is expected to draw large crowds and international teams to stadiums across North America, but questions remain about how organizers will respond if wildfire smoke makes the air unsafe during matches, according to a June 17 report.
SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles has recently come under scrutiny after a series of wildfires led Los Angeles County to issue a multiday air quality advisory. Experts have said that FIFA does not appear to have a clear protocol for handling poor air quality due to smoke if conditions worsen. The issue is especially relevant in Los Angeles, which is scheduled to host eight matches from June 12 to July 10.
“FIFA has basically almost done nothing,” said Nicholas Watanabe, a professor of sport and entertainment management at the University of South Carolina. “They are lagging behind even minor leagues in North America.”
Other sports organizations such as the National Women’s Soccer League, National Collegiate Athletic Association, and National Football League already use Air Quality Index-based guidance and have postponed games because of smoke in recent years. The NFL can relocate games if AQI remains consistently above 200, while the NCAA requires events be moved indoors or canceled once AQI exceeds 300. The NWSL uses a stepped system: hydration breaks at an AQI of 101, consideration of rescheduling at 180, and mandatory postponement or cancellation above 200.
Wildfire smoke poses health risks that can quickly make conditions unhealthy for athletes and spectators—especially children, older adults, and those with respiratory conditions. “They might get a burning throat, a cough, and a headache,” said Mary Johnson of Harvard University’s T.H. Chan School of Public Health.
In response to concerns about climate-related risks at the tournament, FIFA said, “Climate-related risks are assessed as part of overall tournament planning and managed in close coordination with host cities, stadium authorities, and national agencies.” However, FIFA did not specify any AQI threshold for postponing or suspending matches—a point that has frustrated some experts.
“It would make sense for FIFA to think ahead and implement some air quality standards that would trigger some decisions about whether or not to play,” said geographer Dominik Kulakowski. “We’re seeing wildfires become a larger part of life.”
